topics.definition: Hashing is a technique that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values (hash codes) using a hash function. A hash table stores key-value pairs and uses hashing to achieve average O(1) time for insertion, deletion, and lookup.
key_concepts: Hash function: converts a key to an integer index in the hash table
Hash code: the integer output of the hash function
Bucket: a slot in the hash table array where values are stored
Load factor: ratio of stored elements to total buckets — n/m
Collision: two different keys produce the same hash index
Perfect hash function: no collisions — each key maps to a unique index
Uniform distribution: a good hash function distributes keys evenly
Rehashing: resize and rehash all keys when load factor exceeds threshold
from from python_source.content._source.content. hash(): built-in function returning hash code of an object
Hashable: objects that have a hash value — immutable types (int, str, tuple)
important_points: hash() in from from python_source.content._source.content. is randomised per session for strings — not stable across runs
Only immutable objects are hashable: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset
Mutable objects (list, dict, set) are NOT hashable — cannot be dict keys
Load factor > 0.75 typically triggers rehashing in from from python_source.content._source.content. dicts
from from python_source.content._source.content. dicts are implemented as hash tables with open addressing
A good hash function: fast to compute, uniform distribution, deterministic

topics.explanation: Hashing maps keys to array indices for O(1) average-case operations. A good hash function distributes keys uniformly to minimise collisions. topics.definition: A collision occurs when two different keys produce the same hash index. The two main approaches are Chaining (each bucket holds a linked list of colliding entries) and Open Addressing (colliding entries are stored in other buckets using a probing sequence).
key_concepts: Chaining: each bucket contains a linked list of all key-value pairs that hash to that index
Open Addressing: on collision, probe for the next available slot
Linear Probing: check index+1, index+2, ... until empty slot found
Quadratic Probing: check index+1^2, index+2^2, index+3^2, ...
Double Hashing: use a second hash function to determine step size
Clustering: consecutive occupied slots — degrades performance
Primary clustering: problem with linear probing — long runs of occupied slots
Tombstone: marker for deleted slots in open addressing — prevents broken probe chains
from from python_source.content._source.content. dicts use open addressing with random probing
important_points: Chaining: worst case O(n) when all keys hash to same bucket
Linear probing: primary clustering degrades performance at high load
Tombstone prevents breaking probe chains on deletion
Without tombstone: deleting a middle slot breaks subsequent lookups
from from python_source.content._source.content. dict uses open addressing with pseudo-random probing (not linear)
Double hashing eliminates clustering but is more complex to implement

topics.explanation: Collision resolution is fundamental to hash table correctness. Chaining is simple and handles high load factors but has poor cache performance. Linear probing is cache-friendly but suffers from clustering. Tombstones are essential for open addressing deletion — without them, probe chains break and lookups fail.

topics.topic: from from python_source.content._source.content. Dictionaries and Sets
topics.definition: from from python_source.content._source.content. dict and set are built-in hash table implementations. dict maps hashable keys to values with O(1) average operations. set stores unique hashable elements with O(1) membership testing.
key_concepts: dict: hash table mapping keys to values, O(1) average get/set/delete
set: hash table storing unique elements, O(1) average add/remove/in
Both require hashable keys/elements — immutable types only
dict preserves insertion order (from from python_source.content._source.content. 3.7+)
dict.get(key, default): safe lookup — returns default if key missing
dict.setdefault(key, default): inserts key with default if not present
collections.defaultdict: auto-initialises missing keys
collections.Counter: specialised dict for counting
frozenset: immutable set — hashable, can be used as dict key

code_examples.code:
a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
b = {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}
print(a | b)   # union
print(a & b)   # intersection
print(a - b)   # difference
print(a ^ b)   # symmetric difference

fs = frozenset([1, 2, 3])
d = {fs: "my_set"}   # frozenset as dict key

from collections import defaultdict, Counter

graph = defaultdict(list)
for u, v in [(0,1),(0,2),(1,3)]:
    graph[u].append(v)

word_count = defaultdict(int)
for word in "apple banana apple cherry".split():
    word_count[word] += 1

c = Counter("aabbcccdddd")
print(c.most_common(2))
c1 = Counter("aab")
c2 = Counter("abc")
print(c1 + c2)
print(c1 & c2)

important_points: dict.get() is safer than dict[] — no KeyError on missing keys
defaultdict eliminates the need for if key not in dict: dict[key] = [] pattern
Counter is the best tool for frequency counting and anagram detection
Sets are perfect for deduplication and O(1) membership testing
frozenset is hashable — can be used as a dict key or set element
dict.items() returns view objects — they reflect live changes to the dict

topics.definition: Hash table problems use dicts and sets to reduce the time complexity from O(n^2) to O(n). Key patterns: two-sum, anagram grouping, frequency counting, and sliding window with hash maps.
key_concepts: Two-sum: use dict to store seen values and their indices — O(n)
Anagram detection: sort characters or use Counter for signature
Group anagrams: use sorted string as dict key
Subarray sum equals k: prefix sum + hash map — O(n)
Longest substring without repeating: sliding window + set — O(n)
First non-repeating character: Counter + linear scan
Isomorphic strings: two-way character mapping
Frequency-based problems: Counter + heap for top-k elements

important_points: Two-sum hash map: store seen values, look for complement — O(n) not O(n^2)

Sliding window + set/dict: substring problems in O(n)

Always consider if a set or dict can reduce an O(n^2) solution to O(n)

topics.topic: Hash Tables vs Other Data Structures
topics.definition: Hash tables excel at O(1) key-based lookup but do not support ordering or range queries. Trees support ordered operations in O(log n). Arrays support random access in O(1). Choose based on operations needed.
key_concepts: Hash table: O(1) average for insert/delete/search — but no ordering
BST: O(log n) for all operations — supports ordering, range queries, floor/ceiling
Array: O(1) random access, O(n) search — best when index-based access needed
Linked list: O(1) insert/delete at known position — no random access
Trie: O(m) for string operations (m = string length) — best for prefix search
Heap: O(log n) insert, O(1) min/max — best for priority queue
Hash table worst case: O(n) when all keys collide — hash DoS attack

code_examples.description: Set vs list, bisect, heap, trie
code_examples.code:
import heapq, bisect

# Set vs List for membership
data = list(range(100000))
s = set(data)
# s lookup O(1); list lookup O(n)

# Sorted list + bisect for range queries
sorted_data = sorted([5,3,8,1,9,2,7,4,6])
lo = bisect.bisect_left(sorted_data, 3)
hi = bisect.bisect_right(sorted_data, 7)
print(sorted_data[lo:hi])   # [3,4,5,6,7]

# Heap
tasks = [(3,"low"),(1,"high"),(2,"medium")]
heap = []
for p, t in tasks: heapq.heappush(heap, (p, t))
while heap: print(heapq.heappop(heap))

# Trie
class Trie:
    def __init__(self): self.children = {}; self.end = False
    def insert(self, word):
        node = self
        for ch in word:
            node.children.setdefault(ch, Trie())
            node = node.children[ch]
        node.end = True
    def search(self, word):
        node = self
        for ch in word:
            if ch not in node.children: return False
            node = node.children[ch]
        return node.end
    def starts_with(self, prefix):
        node = self
        for ch in prefix:
            if ch not in node.children: return False
            node = node.children[ch]
        return True

when_to_use: dict/set: O(1) lookup, counting, grouping, deduplication
list: ordered data, index access, iteration, small datasets
BST/SortedList: need sorted order + fast search + range queries
Heap: top-k elements, priority queue, k-way merge
Trie: prefix matching, autocomplete, spell checking
Deque: BFS, sliding window, O(1) both-end operations
Counter: frequency counting, top-k, anagram detection
important_points: No single data structure is best for everything — choose based on operations needed
Hash tables do not support: ordering, range queries, predecessor/successor
If you need ordering + fast search: use BST or sorted list with bisect
For top-k elements: Counter + heapq.nlargest is O(n log k)
Trie is O(m) per operation — better than dict for prefix search
